Piggybacking is the term used when you are using power from one circuit, and the neutral from another circuit, to power something. The problem with this is that if you flip off the breaker for the outlet circuit in your kitchen, all it does is cut the hot wire, not the neutral.

But the switch is still powered up from the other circuit, using the neutral from the outlet circuit, which doesn't get disconnected when the breaker is flipped. So if I turned off your kitchen outlets and then went to work on them, I can get shocked by the neutral because you attached your smart switch to it.

Edit: Sometimes electricians will do this just because it saves a little bit on wire. Say I have power at Point A, a new light is at Point B which is 15 feet away, and the switch for the light is at Point C, another 20 feet away. To get the neutral at the switch, I would need to run from Point A all the way to Point C, using 35 feet of wire, then from the switch back to the light, using a total of 55 feet of wire. Or I can run power from Point A to Point B (the light), then drop down to the switch (Point C) without a neutral, using only 35 feet of wire total, saving me 20 feet of wire. Luckily there is a code for this now, and any devices in a finished space have to have a neutral wire at them because of exactly what you are running into, installing smart devices with no neutral at the switch.
